content: The central image depicts fossil fragments identified as belonging to a juvenile Tylosaurus. The holotype of the type species Futalognkosaurus dukei was initially estimated to measure between 32 and 34 meters in length. However, in 2008, this estimate was revised downward to 26 meters. Thomas Holtz later estimated its length at 28 meters, while Gregory S. Paul suggested a maximum length of 30 meters, with a weight ranging between 1 and 50 tonnes. The long neck of Futalognkosaurus contained 14 vertebrae and was over a meter deep in certain areas due to its exceptionally tall neural spines, which had a distinctive shark-fin shape. Its hips were also remarkably large and robust, reaching a width of nearly 3 meters. The genus name Futalognkosaurus is derived from the indigenous Mapudungun language, where futa means giant and lognko means chief. It is pronounced as foo-ta-logn-koh-sohr-us. Futalognkosaurus belongs to the family Titanosauridae (or Lithostrotia, depending on the classification system used) and is most closely related to Mendozasaurus. Together, they define a new clade named Lognkosauria, which includes Futalognkosaurus, Mendozasaurus, their common ancestor, and all their descendants. Malawisaurus is considered the sister group to this clade. Another, much later member of Lognkosauria is the massive Puertasaurus. During the Cenomanian period, the crown group Crocodylia, or true crocodiles, originated. An unnamed enantiornithine bird from northern Gondwana is also known from this time. In 1996, a theropod skeleton was discovered in the Sierra del Portezuelo region of Neuquén Province, Argentina, and reported that same year. In 2002, a second skeleton was uncovered near Lago Barreales and reported in 2003. By 2004, this second specimen was named and described as a new species, Unenlagia paynemili. The holotype, MUCPv-349, consists of a partial skeleton including a humerus, two pubes, and several paratypes: MUCPv-343 (a claw), MUCPv-409 (a partial ilium), MUCPv-415 (a phalanx), and MUCPv-416 (a vertebra). Neuquenraptor may be a junior subjective synonym of Unenlagia. Estimates of Unenlagia's size vary, with some suggesting a length of 5 meters and a weight of 75 kilograms, while others propose a length of just 2 meters. The pelvic region of Unenlagia, particularly the shape of the ilium, closely resembles that of the early bird Archaeopteryx. Initially, its shoulder girdle was interpreted as being adapted for flapping flight, with a flat scapula positioned atop the ribcage, allowing the shoulder joint to point more laterally. However, this would imply that the shoulder blade was dorsoventrally flattened rather than laterally, as seen in other theropods. It is now thought that the scapula was more likely located on the side of the ribcage. This aligns with a later hypothesis suggesting that non-avian theropods like Unenlagia were unable to lift their forelimbs above their backs, a limitation that also applied to the basal bird Archaeopteryx. South American researchers have expressed skepticism about this interpretation, arguing that a laterally positioned scapula would cause the coracoid of Unenlagia to jut into its ribcage, which seems anatomically implausible. Unenlagia was a member of the Dromaeosauridae family and belonged to the highly bird-like Gondwanan clade of dromaeosaurids known as Unenlagiinae. It was closely related to species such as Buitreraptor and Neuquenraptor (which may be the same species as Unenlagia). The flying raptor Rahonavis is also considered part of this group. This suggests that either Unenlagia was secondarily flightless, having evolved from flying ancestors similar to Rahonavis, or that bird-like flight evolved independently at least twice. Rahonavis has been identified as the sister taxon of Unenlagia. However, the Unenlagiidae clade has also been positioned within Avialae. The second image on the right shows a 100-million-year-old piece of amber from Myanmar containing the head, neck, wing, tail, and feet of a hatchling. This specimen provides the most complete and detailed view of its kind ever discovered.
